Stage 3 · Grammar

How often, and where the word goes

The meaning is easy. The position is what learners get wrong.

Read these four sentences from the text.
  • She usually takes fruit and a sandwich.
  • He is always too tired.
  • He never goes to the gym.
  • She goes swimming twice a week.
In the first three sentences, where does the frequency word go?
Where the word goes
PositionExampleWhy
Before the main verbShe usually takes fruit.the normal place
After beHe is always tired.be is the exception
After the auxiliaryHe doesn’t often stop.auxiliary first, then the adverb
Expressions: endShe goes swimming twice a week.the usual place
Expressions: startEvery October, he goes camping.for emphasis
Questions recycledHow often do you go to the gym?  —  the helping verb still comes before the person.
Now put the six words in order, from 100% of the time down to 0%.

FORM. The frequency adverb goes before the main verb — I usually start at seven — but after be: I am usually late. With an auxiliary it slots in after it: I don’t usually work nights.

THE SCALE. always 100% · usually · often · sometimes · hardly ever · never 0%. Hardly ever and rarely mean almost never, not never.

EXPRESSIONS ARE DIFFERENT. Longer phrases — twice a week, every October, once a year — go at the end, or at the start for emphasis. They never sit in the middle.

Not “I go usually to the gym”, not “She never is late”, not “He go every day”.

Questions come back here: How often do you…? is Lesson 1’s word order with a frequency question word in front.

FORM. The frequency adverb goes before the main verb: I usually start at seven. There is one exception, and it is the verb be: with am, is, are, was, were the adverb comes after it — I am usually late, never I usually am late. When there is an auxiliary, the adverb slots in between the auxiliary and the main verb: I don’t usually work nights.

THE SCALE. always 100% · usually about 80% · often about 60% · sometimes about 40% · hardly ever about 10% · never 0%. Two of these trip learners up: hardly ever and rarely mean almost never, not never — and because they are already negative, you do not add another negative. I hardly ever don’t go is wrong.

EXPRESSIONS ARE DIFFERENT. Short adverbs sit in the middle; longer expressions — twice a week, three times a month, every October, once a year — go at the end of the sentence, or at the start if you want to emphasise them. What they never do is sit in the middle: I twice a week go swimming is not English.

The three mistakes to watch: “I go usually to the gym” (adverb after the verb) · “She never is late” (adverb before be) · “He go every day” (missing the third-person -s).

Questions come back here. How often do you go to the gym? is exactly Lesson 1’s order — question word, helping verb, person, main verb — with a frequency question word at the front. You will meet the present continuous against this tense in Lesson 4.

Four real sentences from the coursebook recording.

Full grammar reference — Present Simple and adverbs of frequency

Form

PositiveI / you / we / they work · he / she / it works
NegativeI don’t work · he doesn’t work
QuestionDo you work? · Does he work?
Short answersYes, I do. / No, he doesn’t.
Frequencyalways, usually, often, sometimes, hardly ever, never

Spelling and sound

Third person -s: works /s/ · lives /z/ · watches /ɪz/. Consonant + y → -ies: studies. Irregular: go → goes, do → does, have → has.

When and why we use it

  • Routines and habits: She gets up at six.
  • Things that are generally true: Water boils at 100 degrees.
  • One-word adverbs of frequency go before the main verb but after be: She often works late. / She is often late.
  • Longer expressions go at the end: I go swimming twice a week.

Signal words

every day · on Mondays · once / twice a week · at the weekend · always, usually, often, hardly ever, never

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • He work late. → He works late.Third person needs -s.
  • She doesn’t works. → She doesn’t work.Doesn’t already carries the -s.
  • I go often to the gym. → I often go to the gym.The adverb goes before the main verb.
  • Never I eat meat. → I never eat meat.Never is not a sentence opener here.

Don’t confuse it with

Present Simple = usual. Present Continuous = happening now. Compare She works in Almaty and She is working today. Full contrast in Lesson 4.

Stage 5 · Main input

Reading

Three people, the same twenty-four hours.

Before you read: a night nurse, a freelancer and a farmer.

Who do you think sleeps least? Choose one, then read and find out whether you were right.

No right answer yet. This is your prediction.

The average day — and three people who don’t have one

Every year the American government asks thousands of people one question: what did you do yesterday, hour by hour? The answers become the American Time Use Survey — an average day that almost nobody lives.

A full-time worker works 8.4 hours on a weekday and 5.6 hours at the weekend. Eighty per cent of employed people work on a weekday, but only thirty per cent work at the weekend. They sleep about nine hours and spend nearly five on leisure, half of it television.

That is the average. Here are three people nowhere near it.

Aliya is a night nurse. Her shift runs from seven in the evening to seven in the morning. She hardly ever eats a proper meal at work, and she rarely sleeps well: nurses sleep about eighty-three minutes less before a shift. On her days off she stays in, does the housework, helps her son with his homework and goes swimming twice a week.

Dias is a freelancer. A third of employed people now work from home; Dias does it every day. He writes a to-do list each morning and works indoors until dark. He often works late. He never goes to the gym and gave up running years ago, but he plays chess online twice a week.

Ruslan is a farmer. He gets up early, always, even in winter, and spends the day outdoors. His work is his exercise. In summer he hardly ever has a free weekend, but every October he goes camping.

The survey gives you a number. It does not give you a day. Ask any of the three of them what a normal week looks like, and all three will tell you theirs is completely ordinary.

Sources. All national figures: American Time Use Survey 2024, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — a work of the U.S. federal government and therefore in the public domain. Nurses’ sleep: Witkoski Stimpfel et al., NYU Rory Meyers College of Nursing. The three portraits are written for this course to illustrate the data.
